title: Navigation for a consumer brand
metaTitle: Navigation a new shopper can follow
excerpt: Brand navigation should name shopper jobs in plain words, and one path should reach the product from every page. Mood titles can wait in the footer.
alt: A pale room with an arched opening onto a dark sofa, a low table, and a glass vase of dried stems. A room with an obvious way through, which is what shop navigation should be.
caption: A pale room with an arch onto a dark sofa, a low table, and dried stems. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs in a brand header?
faqs.answer: The jobs a first visit needs: the product or Shop, the real categories in shop language, and a way back to that product from every page. Journal, World, and Explore can wait until they are maintained and useful. Five to seven items is enough.

faqs.question: Where should a seasonal campaign live?
faqs.answer: In a banner with an end date. The header should keep stable nouns so a returning customer can buy a refill without relearning the map. When the banner comes down, the doors should look as they did before.

faqs.question: How should wholesale be treated?
faqs.answer: Give wholesale a footer path if the terms would confuse someone buying one object. The header serves the retail shopper. Two audiences in one menu produce a menu that speaks to neither.

sources.title: Influencing Title Links in Google Search

markdown:
Consumer brand website navigation is a map of jobs a shopper is trying to finish. The labels should be words they already use, and one path should reach the product from anywhere. Department names and mood titles belong in a brand workshop. They make a poor menu for someone who does not know you yet.

A new shopper arrives with an errand. Find the mug. Find the price. Find whether you ship here. The menu should read like those errands.

## Jobs, in shop language

List the jobs before you list the pages you wish you had. See the product. Look at a category they would say out loud. Find shipping and returns. Read who makes it, if they become curious. Ask a question. Each job that a first visit needs becomes a label. A job that serves loyal customers can live one step down.

"Journal," "World," and "Explore" describe the site's self-image. They do not describe the errand. Replace them with the nouns of the catalog. Mugs. Outerwear. Refills. Repair. If one object is the brand, that object's name can be the first label. A shopper should not have to decode you before they can see the thing.

The W3C's [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) are built so content is perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. A menu is an operable, understandable object. Keyboard users should reach every item. The words should say where they go. Icon-only navigation, or a menu that only appears when a mouse hovers, fails people and fails the hurried shopper on a phone at the same time.

Keep the set short. Five to seven items is a map a thumb can hold. Policies, stockists, and a journal can live in the footer until the journal is truly maintained. A top-level Journal that opens on a single old post suggests the shop is a content project that happens to sell something. If the product is the point, the product should occupy the best slot.

## One path to the product

Choose the primary path and repeat it. A header link in stable words: Shop, or the name of the hero object. The destination is the product or a tight collection, with the object and the price shape on the first view. If "Shop" opens an essay, you have inserted a hallway. Hallways make a brand feel large. They delay the only thing a new shopper came to do.

On a phone, the path should be visible without a hunt. A button labeled with the product, sitting in the header, is enough. The full menu can live under a control named Menu, a real name, not an unlabeled icon. The guidelines' demand that controls be understandable applies to that icon as much as to the poetry you were tempted to write beside it.

Use the same product name everywhere. If the homepage said Coast mug, the menu says Mugs or Coast, and the page heading agrees. Synonyms are a small crack. A shopper with two tabs open should not have to decide whether "vessels" and "mugs" are the same door.

The logo can go home. Home should then show the object and the same path within the first view. A logo that lands on a campaign with a different verb breaks the map at the moment someone tries to reorient. Campaigns can be banners. They should not rename the doors.

## Labels that survive a season

Write labels you can keep after the drop ends. "Knitwear" survives. "Autumn edit" expires, and a menu that expires trains people to distrust the chrome. Put the season in a banner with an end date. Leave the navigation stable for the person who bought last year and came back for the refill.

Google's notes on [title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) warn against boilerplate titles and vague labels that fail to say what a page is. Navigation makes the same promise. Menu label, heading, and title should agree. "Repair" in the menu, "Repair a sole" on the page. A menu item called "Care" that opens a manifesto about longevity is a vague gesture. If the page is a service, name the service. If the page is a guide, name the guide.

Test the labels on someone who does not work for the brand. Read the menu and ask where they would tap to buy the object they can see in your advertisement, and where they would tap if the size was wrong. If they hesitate, change the word. Do not add a tooltip to rescue a clever label. Tooltips do not exist for most of the people on a phone.

## What lives one level down

Stockists, press, and a long size guide are real and secondary. Place them where they can be found on purpose. "Size guide" is a good link inside outerwear. It is a poor top-level item if it pushes the product out of the menu. "Download" is never a good link name. Say what the file is.

A journal earns a top-level label only when someone ships it on a schedule you can keep, and when the pieces help a shopper understand the product. A diary of the founder's travels does not earn the slot. Proof pages about a material change can live beside the product they changed, which is a better home than a magazine index nobody opens.

Wholesale is a different audience. Give it a footer link to its own path if the terms would confuse a person buying one object. Two audiences in one menu produce a menu that speaks to neither. The retail shopper is the person the header serves. The retailer can be invited plainly, without taking the first position.

Search belongs in the header when the catalog is too long to scan. On a small catalog, search is an admission that the menu is unclear. Fix the menu first. Add search when you have earned a catalog that needs it. An empty search box above five products looks like a costume borrowed from a larger store.

## The phone menu is the real menu

Design the narrow screen first. A wide bar of links that looks elegant on a desktop often collapses into a drawer that hides Shop. Open the drawer and read the first six items. If the product is sixth, reorder. People scan a drawer from the top, quickly, and they stop when they see a familiar noun.

Give each item a full row. Show the current section. A person already on Mugs should be able to see that, so a second tap does not feel like a broken page. Keep tap targets far enough apart that a thumb reaches Repair only on purpose.

If the drawer animates, keep it short. A menu that performs a long entrance delays the product. Honor reduced motion. The shopper who asked their phone for a still interface includes people with vestibular disorders and people standing in a shop comparing you with the shelf in front of them. Both deserve an immediate list.

A cart link should say how many things are in it, in text, not only as a badge that a screen reader misses. The cart is a job. Name it like a job.

Campaigns will ask to borrow the header. Let them borrow a banner. The header is the map a returning customer uses to buy a refill at 11 p.m., and a map that changes its nouns for a weekend will lose that sale to confusion. Put the campaign's object inside the ordinary label, Shop or the product name, and let the banner carry the season's sentence. When the banner comes down, the map should look as it did before.

If you sell in more than one language or more than one country, keep the job-words parallel. A menu that is concrete in one language and poetic in another is two brands. Pick the concrete set and translate that. The shopper's errand does not become more abstract because the interface changed language.

Match the footer to the header's nouns. If the header says Repair, the footer should not say Care for the same page. Two names for one destination teach the shopper that the site is improvised. Pick the plainer word and use it in both places, including the page heading and the button that returns to it. Repetition here is a kindness, not a failure of variety.


Do that rename once, in a single edit, and then stop. A shop that keeps both words 'for a while' is a shop with two maps, and the phone will show the visitor whichever one loads in the drawer.

## Where the pictures have to live

The menu decides whether photography can argue. If Mugs is a real destination, that page can show the mug clearly. If every object is buried under World, the pictures have nowhere honest to go, and the homepage becomes a collage of moods. The next decision is which frames you will publish, and which manifestos you will refuse to photograph. That is [photography direction for a consumer brand](/blog/photography-direction-for-a-consumer-brand).

Structure is part of the work you can ask a studio to do with you. Look through [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) and notice how few doors a clear shop needs. Bring the jobs your shoppers already try to finish.
